new_statements.quote: The findings of compression placement on Rongga reveal that firstly, the monosyllabic words, whether or not preceded by a consonant, whether or not preceded by a consonant stressed on a single syllable and whether or not preceded by a consonant or before the second syllable, both of which either precedes the consonant or do not follow a word boundary. Second, three and four monosyllabic words will be stressed on the last syllable if they precede the consonant or not.
new_statements.translation: Best-effort de-garbling (NOT reliable): 'Stress ("compression" = tekanan) placement in Rongga: (i) in monosyllables the single syllable is stressed whether or not it has an onset consonant, and [in disyllables] the vowel before the second [= final] syllable is stressed, whether or not an onset precedes, before the word boundary; (ii) three- and four-syllable words are stressed on the last syllable [or: counted from the last syllable?] whether or not an onset precedes.'
new_statements.citation: Suparsa, I Nyoman. 2020 (Vol. 11 No. 4, 2021). "The phonological process of Rongga language from the phonemic into phonetic realization." Journal of Cultural Heritage Management and Sustainable Development 11(4):427-439. Emerald. DOI 10.1108/JCHMSD-01-2020-0012.

new_statements.translation_language: English (author's/publisher's translation of an Indonesian generative stress rule; visibly garbled)
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress in Rongga is rule-governed/predictable (Suparsa treats it as P-rule 14 'penempatan tekanan', not lexical), assigned by syllable count from the word edge regardless of onsets; the abstract seems to say disyllables are stressed on the first (= penultimate) syllable but literally says 3-4-syllable words are stressed on 'the last syllable' -- which would be an odd split and is very likely a mistranslation (e.g. of 'suku kedua dari akhir'). The actual position cannot be fixed from accessible text; Arka 2016 section 4.3 'Tekanan dan Intonasi' or the Emerald full text is needed.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Keywords list 'Primary, Secondary' (stress), implying the article distinguishes primary and secondary stress; no accessible detail.
new_statements.exceptions: None accessible. (Relevant background from Suparsa 2008: schwa /ə/ occurs only word-initially and -medially, never finally, and never in vowel sequences -- the kind of fact that conditions stress exceptions in neighbouring Lio, but no such statement is available for Rongga.)
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule stated over mono-, di-, tri- and quadrisyllabic words (citation forms); Rongga is isolating (no affixes), so word = root.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Rongga proper (ISO ror = rong1269), spoken in Tanarata, Watunggene, Bamo and Komba villages, Kota Komba district, Manggarai Timur, Flores; Suparsa's and Arka's data come from the same community (Arka's ELDP project 2004-06, Suparsa was a project member). Antonius et al. 1997 label the same variety 'bahasa Ngadha dialek Rongga' (i.e. as a Ngadha dialect); Suparsa 2008 and Arka argue it is a separate language. Little internal dialect variation is reported (Elias 2018:84).

sources.citation: Suparsa, I Nyoman. 2008. "The Phonology of Rongga Language: a Transformational Generative Study / Fonologi Bahasa Rongga: Sebuah Kajian Transformasi Generatif" (Udayana dissertation summary, English + Indonesian). Linguistika: Buletin Ilmiah Program Magister Linguistik Universitas Udayana 15 (Sept 2008), 17 pp. [= Glottolog 313897 'E-Journal Universitas Udayana 2009']. Neliti 229701.
sources.note: Lists 14 phonological rules of which no. 14 is 'KF penempatan tekanan' (stress placement rule) and says '[tense] and [stress]' / 'Secara fonetis diperlukan ciri [tegang] dan [tekanan]' are needed phonetically -- i.e. stress is treated as rule-assigned (predictable), but the summary never states WHERE stress falls. Syllable canon V, CV; 6 vowels incl. schwa (no word-final schwa).
